procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated March 7, 1967 of the Bombay High Court, Nagpur Bench in Criminal Revision Application No. 306 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant was convicted on three counts by the Judicial Magistrate. He appealed unsuccessfully to the Sessions Judge. He then filed a revision before the High Court. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on the appellant in respect of contravention of cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Foodgrains (Declaration of Stocks) (Second) Order, 1964, but maintained the conviction for the other two charges, modifying the sentences to imprisonment already undergone and a fine of Rs. 1,000 on each of the two counts.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave. The Supreme Court granted special leave to appeal limited to two points: (1) whether the confiscation of the foodgrains in the house of the appellant was legal.

directions: The order of the High Court maintaining the forfeiture of the seized stock of juar is set aside.

issue.issue_text: whether the confiscation of the foodgrains in the house of the appellant was legal

facts: The appellant was convicted for contravening two orders: the Maharashtra Jowar (Restriction on Purchase and Sale and Control of Movement) Order, 1964, and the Buldana District Juar (Price Control) Order, 1965.
A lower court had ordered the confiscation (forfeiture) of the juar (foodgrains) seized from the appellant's house.
The High Court, while upholding the convictions under these two orders, also maintained the order for the forfeiture of the juar.
law: The appellant argued that the forfeiture was illegal because the two specific orders under which he was convicted did not contain any provision that authorized a court to forfeit the foodgrains themselves.
application: The Supreme Court examined the two relevant orders to see if they provided a legal basis for the forfeiture.
It found that the Maharashtra Jowar Order only allowed for the forfeiture of "packages, coverings or receptacles" in which the juar was found, not the juar itself.
It also found that the Buldana District Juar Order authorized the Collector to *seize* stocks but did not give the *court* the power to *forfeit* them.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that since neither of the orders under which the appellant was convicted contained a provision authorizing the court to forfeit the foodgrains, the order maintaining the forfeiture was illegal and had to be set aside.

issue.issue_text: whether r. 141 (2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962 is not ultra vires the Defence of India Act

facts: The appellant argued that Rule 141(2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962, was ultra vires (beyond the legal power of) the Defence of India Act.
The basis for this argument was that the rule established a rule of evidence that was contrary to the existing law found in Section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act.
law: Section 3(1) of the Defence of India Act grants the Central Government very wide powers to make rules necessary for securing the defence of India, public safety, and maintaining essential supplies.

Section 43 of the Defence of India Act states that the provisions of the Act or any rules made under it shall have effect "notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act."
application: The Court first determined that Rule 141(2) was validly made under the broad powers conferred by Section 3(1) of the Act. It reasoned that providing a method for proving the publication of orders in judicial proceedings was essential to the overall scheme of the Defence of India Rules.
The Court then addressed the argument that the rule was inconsistent with the Indian Evidence Act. It held that this inconsistency did not matter because of Section 43.

Section 43 explicitly allows for rules made under the Defence of India Act to override other existing laws. Therefore, even though Rule 141(2) might be contrary to the Evidence Act, it remains valid and effective due to the overriding power granted by Section 43.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, holding that Rule 141(2) was not ultra vires the Defence of India Act. The rule was found to be within the rule-making power granted by Section 3(1), and Section 43 ensured it would have legal effect despite any inconsistency with the Indian Evidence Act.

arguments.issue_text: whether the confiscation of the foodgrains in the house of the appellant was legal
appellant_arguments: The forfeiture of the juar was illegal because the two orders under which the appellant was convicted, the Maharashtra Jowar (Restriction on Purchase and Sale and Control of Movement) Order, 1964, and the Buldana District Juar (Price Control) Order, 1965, did not contain any provision authorizing the court to forfeit the juar itself.
respondent_arguments: The respondent (the State) was unable to point to any provision in the two relevant orders that authorized the forfeiture of the foodgrains.

arguments.issue_text: whether r. 141 (2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962 is not ultra vires the Defence of India Act
appellant_arguments: Rule 141(2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962, is ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence that is contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act.
respondent_arguments: There is no precedent, either in England or India, where a rule similar to Rule 141(2) has been challenged and declared ultra vires.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Rules made under the Defence of India Act have effect notwithstanding any inconsistency with other enactments. However, a court may only direct the forfeiture of property for the contravention of a specific order if that order itself explicitly provides for such forfeiture.
obiter: The learned counsel has not been able to show us any case in which a rule like r. 141 (2) has been challenged, much less declared ultra vires, both in England and in India.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appeal is partly allowed. The conviction is maintained because Rule 141(2) of the Defence of India Rules is a valid exercise of the rule-making power under the Defence of India Act, and Section 43 of the Act gives it overriding effect over any inconsistent existing legislation like the Evidence Act. However, the order forfeiting the appellant's stock of juar is set aside as illegal because the specific orders under which the appellant was convicted—the Maharashtra Jowar (Restriction on Purchase and Sale and Control of Movement) Order, 1964, and the Buldana District Juar (Price Control) Order, 1965—did not contain any provision authorizing a court to order such a forfeiture.
legal_tests_applied: Whether a rule made under the Defence of India Act is inconsistent with another enactment is immaterial, as Section 43 of the Act gives the rule overriding effect.
To be valid, a rule must fall within the powers conferred by Section 3(1) of the Defence of India Act.
For a court to order the forfeiture of property in relation to a contravened order, the specific order itself must contain a provision authorizing such forfeiture.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that Rule 141(2) is ultra vires because it is contrary to the Indian Evidence Act fails because Section 43 of the Defence of India Act explicitly provides that rules made under the Act shall have effect notwithstanding any inconsistency with other enactments.

Rule 141(2) is valid because it falls within the wide powers given under Section 3(1) of the Defence of India Act, as it is essential to the scheme of the Defence of India Rules, which must necessarily provide for proof of publication of orders in judicial proceedings.
why_respondent_won: Section 43 of the Defence of India Act gives rules made thereunder overriding effect, meaning an inconsistency with the Indian Evidence Act does not invalidate Rule 141(2).
Rule 141(2) is within the rule-making power of Section 3(1) of the Act because it is essential to the legislative scheme, which requires a method for proving that orders have been published.
policy_considerations: For the Defence of India Rules to be effective, they must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and must also provide for a method of proof in judicial proceedings that such publication occurred.
